## Vocabulary

- **self**: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX (23/7)

## How it works

- [statement] Query histories require privacy protection even when identifiers are anonymized. Hearst recommends careful handling and describes opt-in recording with participant removal of information; broader browser activity offers more behavioral context but also captures more sensitive information and requires anonymization and security. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] An IP address or cookie is an uncertain proxy for a person: one person can use several IP addresses, and several people can share an IP address or cookie. Preserve this uncertainty when interpreting apparent task changes or continuity. (medium confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Avoid interpreting shorter elapsed time as automatically better UX. Hearst explains that exploration and refinement can make a successful search experience longer than an unsatisfying one; compare timing with task outcomes and participant evidence. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] A visit or inactivity-delimited session is an operational grouping, not a verified task boundary. Tasks can contain subtasks and interleaved query sequences; temporal proximity alone cannot establish common intent. (medium confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/1935826.1935875
- [statement] Methodological recommendation: document missing actions and context explicitly. Server logs may contain queries without result clicks; browser-level recording can add navigation, while result-page content can strengthen interpretation. Missing click or context data should not be silently interpreted as evidence of failure or confusion. (medium confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.24265v2, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/detecting-good-abandonment-mobile-search/
- [statement] No click does not establish search failure: a results page can satisfy an information need directly. Click, abandonment, and engagement behavior also depend on the answer type, so success proxies require context-specific validation. (medium confidence) — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/detecting-good-abandonment-mobile-search/ · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/final-answer-evaluating.pdf
- [statement] Allow a task to resume after intervening queries and allow related subtasks within a larger task. In the Jones–Klinkner data, a method that ignores hierarchy and interleaving splits queries that belong together; contiguous query runs alone therefore cannot represent all observed tasks. (low confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] A query with no result click can still satisfy the user on the results page. The mobile good-abandonment study uses reading and touch interactions beyond clicks; therefore a no-click episode alone cannot establish task failure or dissatisfaction. (low confidence) — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/detecting-good-abandonment-mobile-search/ · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Methodological recommendation: compare time-based and content-aware boundary assumptions against manually labeled tasks, including nonadjacent query pairs. Report the annotation process and uncertainty rather than treating inferred task labels as directly observed user intent. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/1935826.1935875 · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf, http://sonyis.me/paperpdf/WWW13_camera_fp067-wang.pdf
- [statement] Methodological recommendation: triangulate inferred success and recovery with user evidence and task correctness. A reformulation or renewed search can be part of a continuing task; apparent completion can also conceal an incorrect answer. Trace reconstruction should distinguish continuing effort, task switching, giving up, and verified completion rather than assigning success from the last event alone. (medium confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/good-abandonment/, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/final-answer-evaluating.pdf
- [statement] Zerhoudi and Granitzer explicitly describe their cognitive traces as plausible inferences rather than measurements of mental states. Their study also limits its demonstrated coverage to web search, technical Q&A, and movie recommendations; applying those labels to other UX domains requires further validation. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2602.24265v2 · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] Keep visit or device-session boundaries separate from task boundaries. Jones and Klinkner define a session as a time window, a goal as an atomic information need, and a mission as related information needs; goals and missions can interleave. Treat these as explicit analytical definitions rather than assuming that every session contains one intent. (low confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] Validate a timeout against task labels in the target context instead of treating elapsed inactivity as ground truth. The task-segmentation study finds timeouts inadequate for its general web-search data, while Hearst documents time-, activity-, and reformulation-based alternatives. This evidence does not establish a universal replacement cutoff. (medium confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html
- [statement] Disclose the observation window and what the duration measure omits. Jones and Klinkner note that their bounded observation truncates task-length estimates, and that their duration counts query times rather than clicks or other actions. Such a duration cannot be read directly as total task effort. (low confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Methodological recommendation: define the research question and event coverage before interpreting a search journey. Distinguish recorded query text and time, query reformulations, result clicks, and the result-page context available to the analyst; an event trace is not a complete account of user experience. (medium confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf, https://arxiv.org/html/2602.24265v2, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/personalized-models-of-search-satisfaction/
- [statement] A task episode may resume across session boundaries while other tasks intervene. Analyses restricted to consecutive events within a visit can therefore fragment one information need or combine distinct needs. This is a reason to test cross-session and interleaving assumptions, not to merge every similar query. (medium confidence) — http://sonyis.me/paperpdf/WWW13_camera_fp067-wang.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf
- [statement] Searcher identity is uncertain: one person can use multiple IP addresses and several people can share an IP address. Cookie clearing also changes the observable user pool. Treat a linked identifier as an analysis assumption and report potential splitting or conflation of people. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] Methodological recommendation: preserve the distinction between behavioral association, inferred mental state, and causal evidence. Cognitive labels derived from logs remain interpretations; evaluate subjective experience directly and use appropriate experimental comparisons before attributing satisfaction changes to a design. (medium confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2602.24265v2 · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html
- [statement] The published search research repository by lelugom supplies queries with task ground-truth labels and experiment scripts that repeat cross-validation and statistical significance tests. It is a concrete evaluation lead for session/task inference; its labels do not by themselves verify intent in a different product population. (low confidence) — https://github.com/lelugom/search · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] Treat editorial task labels as inferred intent requiring validation. Jones and Klinkner acknowledge possible editor bias and identify inter-rater reliability and comparison with user self-report as future work. For UX use, compare inferred task groups with participant accounts or observed task performance before trusting them as success or recovery labels. (medium confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html
- [statement] Do not equate a repeated query with a failed refinement or recovery attempt. In the Jones–Klinkner study, immediate repeats could reflect reissuing a query, pagination, refresh, or automatic browser resubmission. Interpretation requires the surrounding event context. (low confidence) — http://www.rosiejonesphd.com/papers/jonesKlinknerCIKM2008.pdf · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
- [statement] Retain uncertainty in satisfaction estimates across people and contexts. Personalized Models of Search Satisfaction reports that satisfied and dissatisfied behavior differs among searchers; the mobile abandonment study shows why click and dwell signals can miss satisfied users. Neither supports a universal behavioral success rule. (medium confidence) — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/personalized-models-of-search-satisfaction/ · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX · also: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/detecting-good-abandonment-mobile-search/
- [statement] Separate descriptive log associations from causal claims about interface changes. Hearst distinguishes ordinary log analysis from comparisons of randomly assigned interface variants and calls for statistical checks and additional studies; even bucket tests make subjective responses hard to ascertain without explicit feedback. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search behavioral-log analysis and session/task inference for UX
